headline: OpenAI nabs Patreon co-founder and two key execs to lead creator product strategy
summary: OpenAI has hired Patreon's co-founder and two former top executives to spearhead its creator product strategy, signaling a potential move into the creator monetization business.
details: OpenAI has officially hired Sam Yam, co-founder and former CTO of Patreon, to lead its Creator Product division. He is joined by Drew Rowny, Patreon's former product head, and Shannon Ma, its engineering head, both of whom recently stepped down.
Yam announced on X that they will build new tools with creators, offering early access. He urged attention to OpenAI DevDay next week, September 29th, where further announcements are expected.

This strategic hiring suggests OpenAI is exploring entry into the creator monetization space, leveraging the expertise of the team that effectively pioneered the creator-subscription economy with Patreon.
The departure of these key executives is a significant blow to Patreon, which recently announced an extensive roadmap for user feature overhauls after laying off 20 percent of its staff in January.
caption:
OpenAI just hired Patreon's co-founder and two top execs. This signals a major new direction for AI-powered creator tools and monetization.

OpenAI has officially hired Sam Yam, co-founder and former CTO of Patreon, to lead its Creator Product division. He is joined by Drew Rowny, Patreon's former product head, and Shannon Ma, its engineering head, both of whom recently stepped down.

Yam announced on X that they will build new tools with creators, offering early access. He urged attention to OpenAI DevDay next week, September 29th, where further announcements are expected.

This strategic hiring suggests OpenAI is exploring entry into the creator monetization space, leveraging the expertise of the team that effectively pioneered the creator-subscription economy with Patreon.

The departure of these key executives is a significant blow to Patreon, which recently announced an extensive roadmap for user feature overhauls after laying off 20 percent of its staff in January.

headline_marked: [[China launches 'Supercomputing-1' AI satellite]] to process Earth data in orbit
headline: China launches 'Supercomputing-1' AI satellite to process Earth data in orbit
summary: The 'Supercomputing-1' satellite processes Earth-observation data in orbit, reducing cross-regional data processing times from hours to minutes by keeping computation local.
details: China has launched nine satellites, including its first integrated "rocket and satellite" AI computing project, as part of its push to put AI computing in orbit. The Kinetica 1 Y18 rocket, operated by CAS Space, lifted off on September 20, carrying the satellites to their planned orbits.

The "Supercomputing-1" satellite, developed by S-AIDC, is designed to capture and process Earth-observation data in orbit. This approach cuts cross-regional data processing times from hours to minutes by keeping the computation local.

The satellite features both a high-resolution optical payload and an image-processing AI computer. This launch highlights China's efforts to develop orbital computing as part of a "broader integrated computing network."

The Chinese government recently approved the Space Computing Industry Innovation Center, aiming to unite rocket and satellite manufacturers, semiconductor fabs, and AI tech companies. This initiative seeks to build a comprehensive space computing network.

The surging demand for artificial intelligence is a key driver for off-planet computing, as terrestrial data centers consume vast electricity and face growing opposition. Space offers advantages like unlimited area, access to solar power, constant cold conditions, and a dead-quiet vacuum.

SpaceX is also a major player in this field with its proposed AI1 satellite, an orbital data center aiming for 150 kW of peak compute power. The company targets 1 GW per year of space AI compute by 2027 and is building a massive facility to manufacture 6,000 satellites for this goal.

Edge compute in space is already useful for applications like Earth-observation satellites processing images onboard to identify wildfires, storms, or ships. This allows sending only useful results back to Earth, rather than enormous amounts of raw data.

This same approach can speed up weather monitoring, disaster response, communications, and even the management of satellite constellations. While a single satellite with edge AI capabilities is not a full orbital data center, China's approach offers a practical and immediate application for advanced computing in orbit.
